name: Mewing appliances
lead: Mewing appliances are oral devices, including palate-expanding plates, mouthpieces, tongue trainers and posture aids, that people use alongside 'mewing', the practice of resting the whole tongue against the roof of the mouth with the lips sealed and breathing through the nose. People who use them are usually aiming for a more forward-set upper jaw, a better-supported midface, a sharper jawline and a more open airway, which they expect to read as a more defined face.[1][16]

Mewing is named after the British orthodontist John Mew (1928-2025) and his son Mike Mew, and belongs to orthotropics, John Mew's theory that tongue, lip and breathing posture guide how the face grows.[17][18] Clinician-prescribed versions of the idea include the Biobloc system, which pairs a palate-expanding appliance with a postural appliance, and in orthodontics more broadly palatal expanders are used to widen the upper jaw.[17][19] Consumer products sold under the mewing banner are a separate category from these clinic-fitted devices.

Interest in the practice rose sharply from 2019, driven by YouTube, TikTok and looksmaxxing forums.[16][8] Orthodontic organisations, including the American Association of Orthodontists, state that tongue posture alone has not been shown to reshape the adult jaw and caution against forcing unnatural tongue positions.[1][20] Proponents say tongue posture matters most during growth, and orthotropic practitioners cite clinic-based cases and the twin study described below.[2] No randomized or controlled trial of over-the-counter mewing appliances in adults appears in the research reviewed for this article; the nearest research concerns clinician-supervised orthodontic and orthotropic treatment, mostly in children, and individual case reports in adults.

paras: Products sold under the mewing banner include flexible palate plates and mouthpieces meant to hold the tongue or lips in position, tongue trainers, and devices marketed as palate expanders. They are distinct from prescription orthodontic expanders fitted by a clinician. The central practice they support, tongue posture, can be done without any device, and tutorials and a tracking app have been promoted from the Mew family's circle.[1]

Popular descriptions of the technique itself, such as WebMD's, tell practitioners to close the lips, rest the tongue flat against the palate with its tip just behind the upper front teeth, keep the teeth lightly together without clenching and breathe through the nose. WebMD adds that any change would be expected to take years.[20] That article does not discuss mouthpieces or appliances, so the device category is documented mostly through forum discussion and product marketing rather than medical sources.

Clinician-prescribed expanders form the relevant medical comparison. Rapid palatal expansion uses a screw-driven device turned by the patient or parent to widen the upper jaw, slower expansion protocols such as MSE spread the change over a longer period, and implant-anchored versions (MARPE) are used in young adults whose palatal suture has already fused; surgically assisted expansion is used for mature palates.[19] Wikipedia lists the reported side effects of expanders as speech changes, excess saliva, headaches, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth and some relapse after treatment.[19]

John Mew was born on 7 September 1928 in Royal Tunbridge Wells and qualified in dentistry at University College London in 1953, followed by specialty training in orthognathic surgery at the Queen Victoria Hospital, East Grinstead, in 1956.[17] In 1958 he proposed the 'Tropic Premise', the view that malocclusion is a postural deformity largely shaped by environment and could be prevented by early correction of oral posture and function.[17][18] In 1968 he visited Rolf Fraenkel in East Germany, who introduced him to Konstantin Buteyko's breathing work, and he went on to develop orthotropics and the Biobloc system, which combines palate expansion with a postural appliance.[17] In 1987 he helped found the International Association of Facial Growth Guidance in Fort Worth, Texas.[17] According to Grokipedia, he also founded the London School of Facial Orthotropics in 1983.[1]

Mew summarised his everyday advice as 'stand up straight and shut your mouth', and the do-it-yourself posture practice was later named mewing after him and his son Michael Gordon Mew.[17] Wikipedia records that Google Trends interest in the term began rising in January 2019 and that The Guardian covered it as a YouTube trend in March 2019.[16] A New York Times Magazine profile of the Mews in 2020 brought the topic to wider audiences.[16] From 2019 the practice was taken up in incel and looksmaxxing communities, and Wikipedia reports that some students were later described as mewing in class.[16]

Mike Mew continued to promote orthotropics and became its most visible advocate on social media. Wikipedia reports that he was expelled from the British Orthodontic Society and that he remained on the dental register as of June 2024.[16][17] John Mew died on 25 June 2025, aged 96.[17]

Orthotropic theory holds that resting tongue pressure on the palate and a closed lip seal influence how the maxilla and mandible grow, so that correct posture encourages forward rather than downward and backward growth. Mew described a 'myofunctionally correct' resting tongue position as applying an outward force that widens the upper jaw and prevents downward and backward maxillary growth.[18] He argued that conventional treatments such as extractions, fixed appliances, elastics and retractive headgear could restrict facial growth.[18]

John Mew published a 1992 paper arguing that orthotropic guidance in children could influence oropharyngeal development and ear ventilation, including through a firm tongue-to-palate swallow.[6] Primate experiments by Egil Harvold are cited by orthotropics supporters as background for posture-driven malocclusion.[1]

Looksmax.org posters describe further proposed effects, for example that holding the tongue up temporarily raises the hyoid bone and gives a crisper jawline outline.[10] Orthodontic summaries hold that such effects are plausible in growing children under appropriate treatment but that evidence of skeletal change in adults from tongue posture or consumer appliances is lacking.[1][17]

In general terms, people combine one or more elements: a tongue-posture habit, nasal breathing, a consumer mouthpiece or tongue trainer, sometimes chewing or jaw-exercise tools, and for some a clinician-fitted expander. Looksmax.org threads show users pairing mewing with palatal expansion, for example a poster with a narrow palate who planned expansion followed by braces.[9][12]

Orthotropic clinics, mostly in the UK, have offered removable expansion appliances and postural appliances to children as an alternative to conventional braces and extractions. Such treatment is practised privately and is not an NHS or General Dental Council-recognised specialty, according to the court judgment described below.[21]

Myofunctional therapy supervised by a clinician is a separate field that addresses tongue posture, breathing and swallowing for specific conditions, and dentists describe it as distinct from consumer gadgets.

A 2007 twin study compared 12 identical twin pairs, one twin treated with fixed orthodontic appliances and the other with orthotropic treatment. Twelve lay judges rated most conventionally treated twins as less attractive after treatment and most orthotropically treated twins as improved. The study came from within the orthotropics literature and was small.[2]

A 2009 case report described condylar bone formation and symptom resolution in a 30-year-old man with a temporomandibular disorder who wore a clinician-prescribed hard acrylic splint that advanced the mandible 2.5 mm; the authors noted that a single case cannot establish causation.[5] A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis examined mouth breathing and atypical swallowing.[7] A 2019 article in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery examined mewing as a social-media alternative to orthognathic surgery, and Wikipedia reports that most orthodontists do not consider it a viable alternative to jaw surgery; a 2026 piece in the Journal of Clinical Orthodontics also addressed the trend.[3][4][16]

The American Association of Orthodontists issued a public warning about mewing in January 2024. Its president, Myron Guymon, said there is no scientific evidence supporting claims of reshaping the jawline, while noting that tongue posture has a role in oral health and development; the AAO lists loosened teeth, bite changes, tooth wear and speech effects among possible risks and advises professional orthodontic assessment.[1][20] Wikipedia notes that reviewers regard parts of Mew's theory as plausible but consider the evidence for effectiveness inadequate.[17]
None of these studies assessed over-the-counter mewing appliances in adults.

John Mew's career included several disputes with regulators. Wikipedia records an NHS fine in the late 1980s that was overturned on appeal to the High Court in 1987, a 2010 General Dental Council reprimand over advertisements judged misleading, and the revocation of his licence in 2017 over false advertising and a patient-confidentiality breach.[17] Mew called himself a whistleblower in the 2010 case.[17]

Mike Mew's General Dental Council case concerned two children treated from 2016 and 2018. According to the High Court judgment, the Professional Conduct Committee decided on 6 November 2024 that his fitness to practise was impaired by misconduct and erased him from the register. It found that treatment with removable expansion appliances, head and neck gear and myofunctional exercises was not clinically indicated for the children, who had normal craniofacial development, that there was insufficient objective evidence to support it, and that claims made in a 2017 YouTube video, including about effects on intelligence, were inappropriate and misleading.[21][22] One child developed a traumatic ulcer from the appliances, and press coverage reported seizure-like episodes in a child.[21][23] Mew responded that the regulator was more concerned about protecting the orthodontic industry.[23]

Mew appealed to the High Court. In a judgment dated 15 May 2026, Deputy High Court Judge Charles Bagot KC dismissed the grounds challenging how the committee treated the expert evidence, including that it was entitled to prefer the General Dental Council's experts over the defence experts.[21] The full disposal of the remaining grounds was not available in the portions of the judgment reviewed for this article.

The American Association of Orthodontists has cautioned that forcing unnatural tongue positions could lead to tooth misalignment, bite problems or speech changes and recommends professional supervision.[1][20] WebMD, summarising expert comments, says that practising the posture is unlikely to cause harm if the teeth are not clenched.[20] Ill-fitting oral devices can cause discomfort or jaw-joint strain, according to dental advice generally. Wikipedia's expander page lists tongue sores, speech changes and relapse among the reported effects of clinician-fitted expanders.[19]
In the High Court judgment, the regulator's panel noted that the clinic-delivered orthotropic treatment was liable to cause harm, although actual harm was not required to prove the charges.[21]

A 2025 qualitative analysis of 8,072 comments on a large looksmaxxing forum found that the community encouraged men to substantially alter their bodies, with mewing named among practices alongside leg-lengthening surgery, and argued that the community's culture is harmful to participants' health.[8] Mewing is among the best-known terms in looksmaxxing vocabulary.

Threads on looksmax.org range from before-and-after accounts, including one about a 20-year-old patient of John Mew, to posts from users who report no visible change after years of practice, and posts about palate expanders as an add-on.[9][11][14] Mainstream coverage has linked the trend to young men's online communities and to the Mew family's clinics.[16]

No studies found on consumer mewing appliances. Related human research includes a 12-pair twin study of orthotropic versus fixed-appliance treatment,[2] an adult splint case report,[5] and a systematic review of mouth breathing and atypical swallowing.[7] Reviews and commentary in oral surgery and orthodontic journals discuss the trend rather than report trials.[3][4]

lore.intro: Mewing is among the most-discussed topics on looksmax.org, where threads range from reports of visible change to reports of no change or of perceived harm, and where palate expanders are often discussed alongside tongue posture.[9][11][13][14]

claims.claim: Mewing produces forward maxillary and chin growth, including in adults.
claims.believers: Threads titled "mewing works and heres how to do it" and "mewing crazy results of forward growth in 20 year old patient of john mew" present before-and-after accounts of forward growth.[14][11]
claims.experts: A 2007 twin study of 12 pairs from the orthotropics literature found lay judges rated most orthotropically treated twins as improved, and the study is described as small.[2] Orthodontic organisations cited in an encyclopedic summary state mewing cannot reliably reshape the jaw, and no trial of mewing in adults has been published.[1] Wikipedia states that no credible scientific research has shown orthotropics to be effective.[16]

claims.claim: Mewing yields at most 1-2 mm in the teen years and mostly acts through a temporary hyoid lift.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org post says mewing at ages 14-17 will do little, to "expect 1-2mm at most," and that it temporarily lifts the hyoid bone for a sharper jawline; another poster, who says they mewed from ages 13-14 and still has a recessed midface, writes that mewing may be "cope."[10][9]
claims.experts: Mainstream orthodontic opinion, as summarised, holds that posture effects are plausible in growing children under supervised treatment but that evidence of skeletal change in adults is lacking.[1] No measurement of a hyoid-lift effect on jawline appearance has been published.

claims.claim: Mewing combined with a palatal expander or MSE improves the midface.
claims.believers: A thread titled "mewing and palatal expander" and the posting of a user with a narrow palate who plans MSE then braces reflect the common pairing of tongue posture with expansion.[12][9]
claims.experts: The article's sources note that clinician-fitted expanders differ from over-the-counter mewing appliances, and no randomized or controlled trial of consumer mewing appliances in adults has been published.[1]

claims.claim: Mewing can damage the face or teeth.
claims.believers: A thread titled "mewing ruined my face" reports perceived harm from the practice.[13]
claims.experts: The American Association of Orthodontists has cautioned that forcing unnatural tongue positions could lead to tooth misalignment, bite problems or speech changes.[1]

claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread titled "mewing lowers anxiety scientific study proof" asserts that a scientific study supports an anxiety benefit.[15]
claims.experts: No cited study has examined mewing and anxiety; the cited reviews address jaw growth, mouth breathing and swallowing.[3][4][7]

claims.claim: Orthotropic treatment is a safer, more natural alternative to braces and extractions.
claims.believers: The Mews and their supporters argue that conventional orthodontics can restrict facial growth and that posture-based treatment guides it in a healthier direction.[17][18]
claims.experts: A General Dental Council panel found orthotropic treatment of two children not clinically indicated and unsupported by sufficient objective evidence, and the High Court dismissed the appeal grounds on expert evidence.[21][22]

claims.claim: Tongue posture can improve the airway and breathing.
claims.believers: Proponents link a high tongue posture and nasal breathing to wider airways, citing orthotropic papers such as Mew's 1992 article on middle ear effusion.[6]
claims.experts: WebMD reports that dentists use related concepts inside broader treatment plans for sleep apnea and misaligned teeth, but that evidence for mewing itself is largely anecdotal.[20]
